11: # Tauri Custom Title Bar
12: 
13: Replacing the OS title bar is the default for a branded Tauri app: the native bar
14: cannot carry your lockup, your palette, or your typography, and it looks pasted-on
15: above a designed surface. This skill covers doing it correctly on desktop — and,
16: just as importantly, **not** doing it on the surfaces where it is wrong.
17: 
18: ## The decision comes first
19: 
20: A custom title bar is a **desktop-window** concern. Before writing one, decide per
21: surface. Never emit it everywhere by default:
22: 
23: | Surface | Window chrome? | What to do |
24: |---|---|---|
25: | **Tauri desktop** (macOS/Windows/Linux) | You own it (`decorations: false`) | Full custom title bar — this skill |
26: | **Plain web / PWA (desktop browser)** | Browser owns it | **No title bar.** The browser already draws one. Add an in-app header only if the design needs a nav/brand strip — with no window controls, no drag region |
27: | **Mobile web / PWA (phone)** | OS + browser own it | **No title bar.** Use a platform app bar (see the mobile navigation guidance) |
28: | **Flutter mobile** | OS owns it | **No title bar.** `AppBar` / `NavigationBar` per platform convention |
29: 
30: If the same React bundle serves both Tauri and the web — the common case in this
31: architecture — the title bar must be **conditionally rendered**, not unconditionally
32: imported. See "Surface gating" below; getting this wrong is a hard crash, not a
33: cosmetic bug.
34: 
35: When the design wants a branded strip on web too, offer the user the choice rather than
36: assuming: (a) no header at all, (b) a plain in-app header sharing the desktop bar's
37: brand tokens but none of its window controls, or (c) a platform app bar on mobile. All
38: three are legitimate; silently shipping the desktop bar to a browser is not.
39: 
40: ## Desktop implementation
41: 
42: ### 1. Turn off the native chrome
43: 
44: ```jsonc
45: // src-tauri/tauri.conf.json
46: "app": {
47:   "windows": [
48:     {
49:       "title": "AppName",
50:       "decorations": false,   // OS draws nothing — you own the whole frame
51:       "transparent": false
52:     }
53:   ]
54: }
55: ```
56: 
57: Once `decorations: false` is set you owe the user **everything** the OS was providing:
58: drag-to-move, minimize, maximize/restore, close, and the accessibility affordances
59: attached to them. Do not set this flag until the component below exists.
60: 
61: ### 2. Platform-correct window controls
62: 
63: Placement is not a style choice — it is muscle memory:
64: 
65: - **macOS** — close/minimize/maximize as traffic lights, **left**, in that order.
66: - **Windows / Linux** — minimize/maximize/close, **right**, in that order.
67: 
68: Detect with `platform()` from `@tauri-apps/plugin-os` and branch. Shipping Windows-style
69: controls on macOS reads as broken to every Mac user.
70: 
71: ### 3. Drag: `data-tauri-drag-region` is not enough by itself
72: 
73: Mark the drag surface with the attribute **and** call `startDragging()` on mousedown:
74: 
75: ```tsx
76: const startDrag = (e: React.MouseEvent) => {
77:   if (e.button !== 0) return          // left button only — right-click is the OS menu
78:   void appWindow?.startDragging()
79: }
80: 
81: <header data-tauri-drag-region onMouseDown={startDrag} className="...">
82: ```
83: 
84: **Why both:** Tauri's built-in webview listener fires reliably only on a direct
85: mousedown against the element carrying the attribute. Flex spacers, wrappers, and the
86: gaps around a centered lockup are *not* that element, so with the attribute alone the
87: bar has dead zones the user experiences as "drag randomly doesn't work." The explicit
88: call makes the whole header draggable. Guard on `e.button !== 0` so right-click still
89: reaches the system menu.
90:
